header.title: FuegoContinuo
header.subtitle: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS hot spots in Argentina (2000 → today).

hero.headline: Fire leaves traces. Let's make them count.
hero.subtitle: Harmonization and scientific exploration of 24 years of satellite thermal observations in Argentina to distinguish climate variability from anomalous fires.
hero.disclaimer: A hot spot is a satellite-detected thermal anomaly in an observation cell, not necessarily an individual fire or its active perimeter. Prior to 2012, calibrated estimates harmonize the scale from MODIS to VIIRS.

methodDialog.title: How we calculate harmonized hot spots
methodDialog.measure: It counts NASA FIRMS satellite thermal detections within the selected area. A hot spot represents a pixel flagged by a sensor. One fire can produce several detections. Measuring individual fires or hectares burned requires other data.
methodDialog.calculationTitle: How we combine MODIS and VIIRS
methodDialog.observation: For each day, we use detections from the designated VIIRS satellite when processing marks it as operational. For the remaining days, we sum available MODIS hot spots by province and month and multiply that count by its conversion factor to the VIIRS scale.
methodDialog.formula: Harmonized count = observed VIIRS hot spots + MODIS-based estimate
methodDialog.referenceSatellites: In the November 14, 2026 data release, S-NPP was the VIIRS reference from January 20, 2012 through November 2, 2026. NOAA-20 is used from November 3, 2026 onward.
methodDialog.calibration: The factor is computed as VIIRS hot spots ÷ MODIS hot spots on days from 2012 onward when every satellite involved recorded hot spots in Argentina. Terra + Aqua was calibrated on 2012–2025, and Terra alone on 2012–2019 (before its orbital drift). Nationally, VIIRS sees 3.0 to 3.9 hot spots per MODIS hot spot depending on the month (≈ 3.3 on average), and 7 to 15 when only Terra is available. The factor varies by province and month of the year; with sparse data it moves toward the regional value and, failing that, the national one.
methodDialog.example: Example from the data published on November 14, 2026: in San Luis, MODIS recorded 208 hot spots in August 2010. With the provincial August factor (3.00), that gives 624.1 VIIRS-equivalent hot spots, with a nominal range of 459 to 774.
methodDialog.observed: Observed: all days in the requested period use the designated VIIRS satellite.
methodDialog.mixed: Mixed: some days use VIIRS counts and other days are estimated from MODIS.
methodDialog.estimated: Estimated: no day in the requested period uses the designated VIIRS satellite.
methodDialog.availability: In the VIIRS layer, “no data” means there was no operational reference in the period. A satellite is treated as available if it records at least one detection in Argentina that day. If MODIS also had no detections on a day that needs estimation, the month reports those days and its confidence drops. A zero does not establish that there was no fire.
methodDialog.uncertainty: The limits come from historical errors grouped by MODIS count (leaving each year out of the calibration). They are applied to the estimated portion, the observed count is added, and the provincial limits are summed for the selected area. For large areas the range is therefore wider than necessary: nationally it contains the true value in almost 99% of months.
methodDialog.validation: In a test fitted on 2012–2019 and evaluated on 2020–2025, the range contained the observed VIIRS count for 77.1% of province-month cases and 64.0% of cases with more than 500 MODIS hot spots. Leaving one year out at a time, coverage is 81%. The monthly error per province is about 15% (about 70% with unharmonized MODIS), and the national annual error is about 4%.
methodDialog.confidence: High: up to 10% estimated days. Medium: the estimate comes from Terra + Aqua, its range is no wider than the estimate itself, MODIS was missing on no more than 10% of estimated days, most of it uses provincial factors, and the area is not mostly in low-data provinces (CABA, Santa Cruz and Tierra del Fuego). Low: everything else, including the whole Terra-only period (November 2000 to July 2002).
methodDialog.comparison: The anomaly compares the harmonized count with the same calendar month in other complete years of the same era: from February 2012 it is compared with years observed by VIIRS; before that, with years estimated from MODIS. The eras are kept apart because MODIS records 33% fewer hot spots in 2012–2025 than in 2003–2011, and mixing them made 35% of recent months come out “below.” With an era-specific reference, each era has 27% of months below and 27% above. At least 10 reference years and a complete target month are required.
methodDialog.comparisonThresholds: The median is the central value. The typical range is the 25th to the 75th percentile. Below the 10th or above the 90th percentile, the category is “far below” or “far above.”
methodDialog.limitBeforeViirs: VIIRS did not exist before 2012, so applying today’s MODIS–VIIRS relationship to 2000–2011 is an assumption. It is supported by the factor showing no trend over 2012–2025, but it cannot be measured directly. Whether the drop in MODIS hot spots between eras is real or a sensor effect is also unverified.
methodDialog.limitAvailability: “Operational” means at least one hot spot nationwide that day. Comparing S-NPP with NOAA-20 found 31 days with partial coverage that still count as observed (about 7,000 missing hot spots).
methodDialog.limitOrbit: Since 2022 the Terra and Aqua orbits have drifted: their overpass time shifted by about an hour by 2025. The combined Terra + Aqua factor shows no trend, but each satellite on its own does.

payload.name: Payload (Optical Sensor)
payload.specs: MODIS: 36 bands (1 km) · VIIRS: 22 bands (375 m)
payload.desc: Electro-optical radiometer with cryogenic infrared detector and scanning mirror to measure thermal radiance and detect active hot spots.

solar.name: Solar Power & Batteries
solar.desc: Steerable solar wings track the sun during daytime passes and recharge Ni-H2 / Li-Ion batteries for orbital eclipses.

thermal.name: Thermal Control (MLI & Radiator)
thermal.specs: Gold MLI blankets · Passive cooler < 85 K
thermal.desc: Multilayer insulation (Kapton MLI) and radiator panels radiate heat to deep space to keep infrared detectors cryogenic.

comms.name: Communications & Telemetry
comms.specs: X & S-band parabolic antenna · TDRSS link
comms.desc: Continuous downlink of scientific telemetry packets and direct broadcast commands to ground stations and relay satellites.

aocs.name: Attitude & Navigation (AOCS)
aocs.desc: Star trackers and gyroscopes maintain nadir pointing toward Earth's surface with sub-pixel pointing accuracy.

propulsion.name: Orbital Propulsion
propulsion.desc: Orbit maintenance thrusters compensate for atmospheric drag and preserve equatorial crossing solar time (10:30 AM / 1:30 PM).
